segments.text: What's up guys, welcome back to CrimeTimeSnacks.
Before anyone opened Meredith Kercher's locked bedroom door, police arrived at her apartment to ask about an abandoned phone, and it turned out to be hers.
Sit with that for a second.
The officers who showed up that day were police telecommunications investigators, and they'd come to ask about a phone.
Meredith Kercher was a 21-year-old British exchange student from London.
She was spending a year in Perugia, Italy, studying abroad.
Perugia's a university town of about 150,000 people, and more than a quarter of them were students, many from overseas.
She lived in a four-bedroom flat at Via della Pergola 7.
She moved in on September 10, 2007.
One detail stays with me.
Meredith typically called her mother every day.
In November 2007, Meredith was killed in that flat.
She was found in her own bedroom on November 2.
She'd been stabbed, and the cause of death was blood loss from wounds to her neck.
That's all we'll say about it for now, and it's enough.
Now for the name you already know.
Amanda Knox was Meredith's roommate.
She was 20 years old, an American from Seattle, a student at the University of Washington.
She'd come to Perugia for an exchange year at the University for Foreigners, and she moved into the flat on September 20, ten days after Meredith.
That's when the two of them met for the first time.
You've probably heard the headline version of what came next.
Here's the snack-sized outline of what the record actually shows.
Knox was convicted of Meredith's murder in 2009 and sentenced to 26 years.
In 2011, that conviction was overturned and she went home to America.
Then it reversed again.
In 2013, Italy's highest court overturned the acquittal and ordered a retrial.
In 2014, an appeals court in Florence convicted Knox a second time.
And in 2015, the Supreme Court of Cassation definitively acquitted her of Meredith's murder.
So from 2007 to 2015, this case kept Italian courts busy for the better part of a decade.
Convicted, acquitted, convicted, acquitted.
The world watched every swing of it.
Here's what I want you to keep in mind as we go.
Underneath all the noise, there's a young woman who came to Italy to study.
Her father, John Kercher, wrote a book about her called Meredith.
So let's unpack it carefully, starting with that phone.
I want to back up.
Way up.
Because the young woman who became the subject of intense media attention started out somewhere very ordinary.
Amanda Knox was born on July 9, 1987, in Seattle, Washington.
Her full name is Amanda Marie Knox.
One account describes her as the eldest of three daughters.
Another lists one younger sister, Deanna, and two stepsisters.
Her mother is Edda Mellas.
She's a mathematics teacher, and she's originally from Germany.
Her father is Curt Knox.
He worked as a vice president of finance for Macy's.
So you've got a math teacher on one side and a finance executive on the other.
Amanda and her sisters grew up in West Seattle.
One account calls the area she grew up in a middle-class neighborhood.
Her parents split up when she was young.
Here's where the sources don't quite line up.
One says they divorced when she was a child.
Another says it happened when she was a toddler.
Those aren't wildly different, but I'm giving you both, because I'm not going to pick one and pretend the other doesn't exist.
Her mother later married Chris Mellas, an information-technology consultant.
I'm spending time here on purpose.
Before the trial, a best-selling Italian book would be telling a very different story about who Amanda Knox was.
Some of it would be imagined or invented outright.
So it helps to start with what the record actually shows about her early life, which is pretty simple.
A girl from West Seattle.
A teacher's daughter.
That's the starting point.
Everything else got layered on later.
The first time Amanda Knox saw Italy, she was 15.
It was a family holiday, nothing more than that.
But it's where the road to Perugia really starts.
On that trip she saw Rome.
She saw Pisa.
She saw the Amalfi Coast and the ruins of Pompeii.
That's a lot of Italy for one teenager to take in, and by the record's account, some of it stuck.
Her mother gave her a book.
It was Under the Tuscan Sun.
After reading it, she grew more interested in the country.
It's a small detail, but I like it, because it's the kind of thing that actually shapes a kid's plans.
A trip, a book from your mom, and suddenly a place feels like it could be yours.
Then comes the part that looks like any other student's life.
She graduated from Seattle Preparatory School in 2005.
One account calls it Seattle Preparatory High School, but it's the same school either way.
That fall she started at the University of Washington, and she chose linguistics.
She did well there.
In 2007, she made the dean's list.
She also held down part-time jobs.
Here the accounts frame the money a little differently.
One says she worked to fund an academic year in Italy.
Another says she worked several jobs to pay her tuition.
Both could be true, and I'm giving you both.
One account sums her up as, by all appearances, an ordinary college student.
She threw loud parties.
She made the dean's list.
Friends remembered her as kind and gentle.
That's the snack-sized version of who she was at 20.
Now here's the detail I want you to hold on to.
Relatives described her as outgoing but unwary.
Those two words sit side by side for a reason.
Her stepfather had strong reservations about her going to Italy that year.
His reason was simple.
He found her too naive.
But it's worth noting that someone in her own family thought she wasn't ready.
She went anyway.
She'd worked part-time jobs to fund the year.
So the plan was set, and the next stop was Perugia.
So why Perugia?
According to the record, she chose it for its universities, and because it had fewer tourists than Florence.
Florence was the more popular pick for foreign students.
Perugia was the quieter option, and that was part of the appeal.
You already know the address, the flat where she'd meet Meredith for the first time that September.
Here's one detail the sources don't agree on.
One account calls it a ground-floor apartment, and another calls it a first-floor flat in a house.
I'm giving you both.
Four women lived there.
Two were Meredith and Amanda.
The other two were Italian women in their late twenties, and one account describes them as trainee lawyers.
One of them was Filomena Romanelli.
Remember that name.
When that locked bedroom door comes up again, she's going to be standing right there in the flat.
The other flatmate is named in one account as Laura Mezzetti.
So picture the setup.
Two foreign students in their early twenties, one British and one American.
Two Italian women a little older, further along in their lives and their training.
Everyone sharing one flat.
Knox also picked up a part-time job.
She worked at a bar called Le Chic.
One account calls it a pub, but it's the same place.
The owner was a Congolese-French man named Diya Patrick Lumumba.
That's the only thing I'm going to tell you about him right now, beyond this.
He's going to matter a great deal later in this story.
Now, here's a detail that gets overlooked in the headline version.
Living under the same roof didn't mean Meredith and Amanda ran in the same circle.
Meredith had a group of English friends in Perugia.
According to the record, those friends saw relatively little of Knox.
The reason given is simple.
Knox preferred to socialize with Italians.
I want to be careful here.
It's just two young women in a new city, each finding her own people.
But keep it in mind.
For now, it's a snack-sized fact about a roommate with her own social life.
So that's the flat.
Four women, a new job at a bar, and two separate circles of friends.
And there was more going on in that building than just the four of them.
Below the flat, there was another apartment.
It was a walk-out semi-basement, set into the lower level of the same house.
One account says four young Italian men lived down there, and both Meredith and Amanda were friendly with them.
One of those men was Giacomo Silenzi.
He shared an interest in music with both women.
He often came up to visit their apartment, so this wasn't a case of neighbors nodding on the stairs.
The two floors of that house were social with each other.
Now I want to slow down on one night in mid-October.
Knox and Kercher had been out, and they got back to the house around 2 a.m. They didn't go straight upstairs.
They ended up in the basement apartment.
Here's who was there.
By one account, it was Knox, Kercher, Silenzi, and another young man who lived downstairs.
And there was a visitor.
His name was Rudy Guede.
Guede wasn't a stranger to the men downstairs.
He was someone they knew from the basketball court.
Another account puts it a little differently.
It says some of the Italian tenants had invited him into the lower-level flat, and that's where the two women met him.
Either way, the picture is the same.
Two roommates come home late, stop in at the neighbors' place, and a friend of the guys downstairs is sitting there.
That's how Meredith Kercher and Amanda Knox met Rudy Guede that night, according to the record.
The night went on for a while.
At 4:30 a.m., Meredith left.
She said she was going to bed.
Knox followed her out.
Guede didn't leave.
He spent the rest of that night in the basement apartment.
On its own, that's not remarkable.
Young people in a university town stay up late and crash on friends' couches all the time.
And it wasn't the only time.
Knox later recalled a second night out with Kercher and Silenzi.
On that night too, Guede joined them downstairs in the basement apartment.
So hold on to the shape of this.
Guede wasn't someone who'd never been near that house.
He'd been in the basement apartment on two nights, with Kercher and Knox both there.
He was a basketball court acquaintance of the Italians who lived downstairs.
That's what the evidence actually shows about how these lives overlapped.
A shared house, a friendly basement, late nights, and a man from the basketball court who'd stayed downstairs after the women went up to bed.
Keep that basement in mind, because it's part of this house's story now.
Now let's move through the rest of October.
It's a short stretch of calendar, but a lot changes in it, and most of it looks completely ordinary.
About three weeks before her death, Meredith went with Amanda to the EuroChocolate festival.
One account places it in mid-October.
It's exactly what it sounds like, a chocolate festival in a university town, and the two roommates went together.
I want you to notice that.
A lot of people would later insist these two didn't get along.
Here they are, a few weeks into living together, out at a festival side by side.
Then comes October 20.
Meredith went to a nightclub with a small group, and Amanda was part of that group.
So was Giacomo Silenzi, the music-loving neighbor from downstairs.
After that night out, Meredith and Silenzi became romantically involved.
Later that same day, Rudy Guede visited the basement again.
The record just notes the visit and moves on, so I'm not going to make it mean more than it does.
Five days later, on October 25, Meredith and Amanda went to a concert together.
One account calls it a classical music concert.
That's where Amanda met Raffaele Sollecito.
He was 23.
Now here's where the sources describe him a little differently.
One calls him a software engineering student.
Another says computer science at the University of Perugia, and a third says computer engineering.
Either way, he studied computers, and he was a few years older than Amanda.
One account adds a bit more.
It says that following Kercher's early departure, Knox began talking to him.
She'd later describe him as an "Italian Harry Potter."
According to that same account, he later stopped by Le Chic, the bar where she worked, and that's what set the relationship in motion.
It moved fast.
The record calls it brief but intense.
They started dating soon after that concert.
And Amanda began spending her time at his flat.
It was about a five-minute walk from Via della Pergola 7.
Close enough that going back and forth between the two places was easy.
So step back and look at where everyone stood by late October.
Meredith was seeing Silenzi, the man downstairs.
Amanda was spending her time at Sollecito's place, a short walk away.
None of that is sinister.
It's two young women a few weeks into a year abroad, each starting something new.
But those five minutes between the two flats are going to matter when we get to the first of November.
November 1 was a public holiday in Italy.
All Saints' Day.
And on that day, the house emptied out.
The Italians who lived there were away.
One account says Meredith's Italian flatmates and the young men from the basement were all out of town.
Meredith spent that evening with friends.
One account says she watched a movie at a friend's house.
Another says she had dinner with three English women at one of their homes.
I'm giving you both.
One account says she parted company with a friend around 8:45 p.m., about 500 yards from the flat.
She's believed to have gotten home around 9.
And if that's right, she was alone in the building.
Now jump to the next morning.
Amanda Knox's account is that she'd spent the night at Sollecito's.
She was the first person to come back to the flat the morning after the murder.
Here's what she says she found.
The front door was open.
There were bloodstains in the bathroom she shared with Meredith, and one of them was a footprint.
Another account describes it as drops of blood.
And Meredith's bedroom door was locked.
One account adds that Knox guessed Meredith was sleeping.
A locked door, on its own, can mean that.
But hold on to the full picture: an open front door, blood in the bathroom, and a door that wouldn't open.
Just after midday on November 2, Knox called Meredith's English phone.
Nobody answered.
And the record notes that wasn't normal for Meredith.
Not answering her phone was out of character.
So Knox picked up her phone again.
This time she called Filomena Romanelli, one of her flatmates.
She spoke to her in a mix of Italian and English, and she said she was worried something had happened to Meredith.
She told Romanelli what she'd seen at the flat earlier that morning.
The open door.
The blood in the bathroom.
The locked bedroom.
One more thing on timing, because the sources don't line up neatly.
One account says she noticed all of this earlier that morning, before the call.
Another says she and Sollecito got back to the flat around noon and found it then.
I'm not going to choose between them.
Just keep both in mind, because the order of that morning is going to get a lot of attention.
After that call to Romanelli, Knox and Sollecito went to Via della Pergola 7.
At Meredith's locked door, they tried to get an answer from her.
There was nothing.
No voice, no movement, no reply.
So they tried to get in.
According to the case file, they attempted to break the bedroom door open.
It didn't work.
What they did leave behind was damage.
The record says the door was noticeably damaged by the attempt.
A damaged door is the kind of detail that gets read a lot of different ways later on.
Now the clock starts to matter, so I'm going to give you the times exactly as the record has them.
At 12:47 p.m., Knox called her mother back in Seattle.
That's Edda Mellas, the math teacher we talked about at the start.
Her mother's advice was simple.
Contact the police.
One quick note on the order of things.
One account lists Knox's calls as Meredith's phone first, then the roommate, then her mother.
That lines up with what the case file shows, so on this stretch the sources mostly agree.
Four minutes later, at 12:51 p.m., Sollecito got through to the Carabinieri.
If you're not familiar with Italy, the Carabinieri are the national gendarmerie.
That call was recorded.
So for once in this case, we don't have to rely on anybody's memory of what was said.
We have what Sollecito actually told them.
He reported a break-in.
But he said nothing had been taken.
Then he laid out what he called the emergency.
Meredith's door was locked.
She wasn't answering calls to her phone.
And there were bloodstains.
Think about how that reads.
A break-in where nothing's missing.
A locked door.
A young woman who isn't picking up.
Blood in the flat.
Each piece on its own might have an innocent explanation, but put together, it's a call for help.
And here's the part that connects back to where we started.
Sollecito had made his call to the Carabinieri.
But the officers who turned up at the flat were those phone investigators.
So at this point, there were two separate threads.
A recorded call asking for help with a locked door, and the police who'd arrived about Meredith's Italian phone.
So let's go back to the police at the door.
One account describes them as two officers whose experience was in investigating postal crimes, not murders.
Another account says they were the telecommunications investigators, and the abandoned phone turned out to be Meredith's Italian phone.
Then Filomena Romanelli arrived.
Knox's call had brought her back to the flat, and once she got there, she took over.
She explained the situation to the officers herself.
Now the phones start to fit together.
The police were told about Meredith's English phone.
It had been handed in because it rang, and it rang because Knox had called it just after midday.
Here's where the sources differ.
One account says it was the English phone that had been found dumped.
Another says a neighbor found both of the phones Meredith normally carried, in a nearby garden.
Either way, Meredith's phones were outside the house, and she wasn't answering.
That's when Romanelli became concerned.
And there's one more detail.
She moved through the flat looking for anything missing, and in doing that, she unintentionally disturbed the crime scene.
That detail matters later.
Romanelli asked the officers to force the door open.
They declined.
According to one account, they didn't think the circumstances justified damaging private property.
Think about where everyone stood.
Knox and Sollecito had already tried to break that door in and failed.
Now the police were standing in front of it, and they wouldn't break it either.
So the door got opened another way.
One account says a male friend of Romanelli kicked it in, around 1:15 p.m. Another account says the officers themselves kicked it down.
I can't tell you which is right.
I'm giving you both.
Inside, Meredith Kercher was lying on the floor of her bedroom.
Her body was covered by a duvet.
I'm not going to add more than that.
Once it opened, everything about that flat changed.
The door and the blood weren't puzzles anymore.
They were evidence in a murder case.
Knox and Sollecito sat in prison for more than a year before a trial even started.
When it finally opened in Perugia on January 16, 2009, they'd been locked up for 14 months.
The court was a corte d'assise.
Judge Giancarlo Massei presided, with Deputy Judge Beatrice Cristiani, alongside six lay judges.
The charges included murder, sexual assault, carrying a knife, simulating a burglary, and theft.
Both Knox and Sollecito pleaded not guilty.
There was a second matter running alongside it, heard by the same jury.
Knox was also accused of falsely accusing her employer at the bar, Patrick Lumumba.
Her police interrogation was ruled inadmissible in the murder trial.
But it was heard in that separate case.
The trial ran for more than 50 hearings, with dozens of witnesses.
Knox took the stand herself.
She repeated her account of that night.
She also rejected the claim that she and Meredith didn't get along.
On December 5, 2009, the verdict came in.
Sollecito was convicted too.
Knox was sentenced to 26 years.
Sollecito got 25.
The two were also ordered to pay more than $7 million to Meredith's family, and Knox was ordered to pay Lumumba around $60,000 for defamation.
That could've been the end of it.
It wasn't.
In November 2010, their appeal opened before Judges Claudio Pratillo Hellmann and Massimo Zanetti.
Here's what the evidence actually shows about that appeal.
The court ordered independent experts to review the contested DNA.
They found numerous basic errors in how it was gathered and analyzed.
And they concluded there was no evidential trace of Meredith's DNA on the alleged murder weapon.
On October 3, 2011, Knox and Sollecito were acquitted.
The court had a middle option available, something close to a verdict of not proven.
It didn't use it.
It acquitted them completely.
In their written report, the appeal judges said the original guilty verdict "was not corroborated by any objective element of evidence."
They noted that Judge Massei had used the word "probably" 39 times in his ruling.
And they found no evidence of any calls or texts between Knox or Sollecito and Rudy Guede.
One conviction did survive.
The slander charge over Patrick Lumumba was upheld, and the sentence went from one year to three years and eleven days.
Knox was released.
On how long she'd been held, the sources put it slightly differently.
One says four years, another says nearly four.
Either way, she walked out and went home to America.
Remember the snack-sized outline from the start, though.
This wasn't over.
Prosecutors weren't done.
According to one report, four months after the conviction was overturned, they appealed the acquittal to the Supreme Court of Cassation.
On March 26, 2013, that court set the acquittals aside.
One account says it declared the appeal verdicts null for "manifest illogicalities."
The court said the Hellmann appeal had gone beyond its remit.
It hadn't ordered new DNA tests, and it hadn't given weight to circumstantial evidence in context, like Knox's accusation against Patrick Lumumba in those disputed interviews.
There was one more piece.
Knox had written a note in the police station, and it didn't mention Rudy Guede.
The Supreme Court read that note as confirmation that she and Guede were both at Via della Pergola 7 while Meredith was attacked.
A retrial was ordered.
Knox was 25 by then and back in Seattle, about to release a book about her ordeal.
She responded with a statement.
She said the ruling came "when the prosecution's theory of my involvement in Meredith's murder has been repeatedly revealed to be completely unfounded and unfair."
The new trial went to an appeals court in Florence.
It opened three months after the Supreme Court published its reasoning, which criticized the "deficiencies, contradictions and illogical" conclusions of the earlier appeal.
Knox had lawyers there representing her.
She stayed in the United States, and Sollecito wasn't in court either.
Judge Nencini presided.
He granted a prosecution request to test a DNA sample from Sollecito's kitchen knife that had never been examined.
That's the knife the prosecution called the murder weapon, the one the independent experts had already undercut at the earlier appeal.
When that new sample was tested, no DNA belonging to Meredith was found on it.
The jury deliberated for eleven and a half hours.
Then Knox and Sollecito were convicted of murder a second time.
One account dates the verdict January 30, 2014, and another says February 2014.
I'm giving you both.
The judge added two and a half years to Knox's sentence.
In practical terms, the two of them were in very different spots.
Sollecito was ordered to surrender his passport.
Knox was legally in Seattle, and extradition would only become a real question if the ruling was upheld.
The written explanation is worth hearing.
The judges pointed to Guede's separate fast-track verdict as a reference point establishing that he hadn't acted alone.
The report said there must have been a cleanup that removed traces of Knox from the building while leaving Guede's.
And it said there'd been no burglary at all, that the signs of one were staged.
So the conviction was back on the books, and Knox was an ocean away.
So let's talk about what was happening outside the courtroom while all of that played out.
Because the case wasn't only argued in front of judges.
It was argued everywhere.
Amanda Knox came to international prominence during her trial.
Before Perugia, she was a linguistics student from West Seattle.
The 2009 trial and her conviction were highly publicized.
The presiding judge allowed the proceedings to go ahead with the media present, but with no live television coverage.
That didn't slow anything down.
One account describes it plainly as a media frenzy, one that turned Knox into a household name.
And a lot of that coverage leaned on a nickname.
Foxy Knoxy.
According to her parents, it started on the soccer field when she was a kid, because of her athletic skill.
In the press, it meant something else entirely.
One account says that portrayal painted her as promiscuous and manipulative, and that it fueled both public interest and bias.
I want to be clear about what that means.
A childhood sports nickname got recycled into a character, and that character was put in front of people who were also being asked to think about a murder.
That's not neutral coverage.
And it wasn't fair to the person on trial.
Then came 2011.
Her acquittal, two years after the conviction, was highly publicized too.
The convictions had already been met with significant criticism, particularly over how the forensic evidence was handled and whether the trial was fair.
Notice what that does to the people following along.
It's hard for anyone to separate what the evidence actually shows from what they've been told to feel about it.
Then there's the cartwheels.
A story circulated claiming that Knox did cartwheels in the police station after Meredith's death.
Think about what that kind of detail does.
What it tells you is how someone supposedly behaved, and then it invites you to decide what that behavior means.
And through every round of it, the person who was murdered was Meredith Kercher.
So the Florence conviction was the last guilty verdict, and it didn't hold.
That 2015 Cassation ruling overturned Sollecito's conviction too.
That's where the murder case against Amanda Knox ends.
One conviction stayed on the books.
The court left in place her defamation of Lumumba.
And later coverage reports that an Italian court reconvicted her of slander in a new trial over that accusation, though she wouldn't serve more time for it.
Knox released a statement after the final ruling.
She described herself as "tremendously relieved and grateful."
Her Italian lawyer said the outcome of a case that had run nearly eight years "couldn't be better than this."
So what came after?
Knox has written two memoirs about her life.
She's worked as a podcaster and public speaker.
She executive produced a 2025 show called The Twisted Tale of Amanda Knox.
She married Christopher Robinson, and they have two children.
And she started doing stand-up comedy.
That's not a typo.
The woman who was the subject of intense international media coverage now gets on stage and tries to make people laugh.
In 2026, Knox announced a comedy show at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival.
It focuses on the events in Perugia.
The show is called Cartwheel.
You already know where that title comes from.
So here's the question I'll leave with you.

You could also look at it from the other side of the case.
Because there's another family in this story.

Both of those things are true at the same time, and I'm not going to tell you how to weigh them.
Read the file.
Form your own conclusion.
